@@@ USER
How do I run many async tasks in JavaScript but only a few at a time (a concurrency limit)?
@@@ ASSISTANT
`Promise.all` on everything starts all tasks at once, which can overload a server or hit rate limits. Instead start a small number of "workers". Each worker repeatedly takes the next task from a shared list until none are left.

```js
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function runPool(tasks, limit) {
  const results = new Array(tasks.length);
  let next = 0;

  async function worker(id) {
    while (next < tasks.length) {
      const index = next++; // safe: JavaScript runs this line without interruption
      results[index] = await tasks[index](id);
    }
  }

  const workers = Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, tasks.length) }, (_, i) => worker(i + 1));
  await Promise.all(workers);
  return results;
}

const makeTask = (name, ms) => async (workerId) => {
  console.log(`worker ${workerId} start ${name}`);
  await sleep(ms);
  console.log(`worker ${workerId} done  ${name}`);
  return name.toLowerCase();
};

runPool(
  [makeTask("A", 400), makeTask("B", 100), makeTask("C", 200), makeTask("D", 50)],
  2
).then((results) => console.log(results));
```

Output:

```
worker 1 start A
worker 2 start B
worker 2 done  B
worker 2 start C
worker 2 done  C
worker 2 start D
worker 2 done  D
worker 1 done  A
[ 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' ]
```

How to read it:
- Only two tasks run at any time. Worker 2 finishes its short tasks and keeps taking new ones while worker 1 is busy with the long task A.
- Results are stored by index, so they come back in the original order even though the tasks finished in a different order.
- To use it for downloads, make each task `() => fetch(url).then((r) => r.json())` and choose a limit like 4 to 8.
- If a task can fail, wrap its body in `try/catch` and store `{ error }`, otherwise the first rejection stops that worker and rejects the whole `Promise.all`.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Write a small event emitter class in JavaScript with on, off, once and emit, and explain how it works.
@@@ ASSISTANT
An emitter keeps a map from event names to lists of handler functions. `emit` calls every handler registered for that name.

```js
class Emitter {
  #handlers = new Map(); // private field: outside code cannot touch it

  on(event, fn) {
    if (!this.#handlers.has(event)) this.#handlers.set(event, []);
    this.#handlers.get(event).push(fn);
    return () => this.off(event, fn); // returns a function that unsubscribes
  }

  off(event, fn) {
    const list = this.#handlers.get(event);
    if (!list) return;
    this.#handlers.set(event, list.filter((handler) => handler !== fn));
  }

  once(event, fn) {
    const wrapper = (...args) => {
      this.off(event, wrapper);
      fn(...args);
    };
    return this.on(event, wrapper);
  }

  emit(event, ...args) {
    // copy the list first, so handlers that unsubscribe while running do not skip others
    for (const fn of [...(this.#handlers.get(event) ?? [])]) fn(...args);
    return this;
  }
}

const bus = new Emitter();
const stop = bus.on("greet", (name) => console.log("hello", name));
bus.once("greet", (name) => console.log("first greeting only for", name));

bus.emit("greet", "Asha");
bus.emit("greet", "Ravi");
stop();
bus.emit("greet", "Meena"); // nobody is listening any more
console.log("done");
```

Output:

```
hello Asha
first greeting only for Asha
hello Ravi
done
```

Where this pattern is useful:
- Separating parts of an app: the cart emits `"item-added"`, and the header badge, the analytics code and the toast message each listen, without the cart knowing about them.
- Node.js has this built in: `const EventEmitter = require("events");`. Use the built-in one in real projects; writing your own once is the best way to understand it.
- Always remove listeners when a component is destroyed (`stop()`), or old handlers stay in memory and run twice.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Implement an LRU cache in JavaScript.
@@@ ASSISTANT
An LRU (least recently used) cache holds a limited number of items and, when full, throws away the one that was used longest ago. A JavaScript `Map` remembers insertion order, so the first key is always the oldest. To "refresh" an item, delete it and insert it again, which moves it to the end.

```js
class LRUCache {
  constructor(limit) {
    this.limit = limit;
    this.map = new Map();
  }

  get(key) {
    if (!this.map.has(key)) return undefined;
    const value = this.map.get(key);
    this.map.delete(key); // move to the "newest" end
    this.map.set(key, value);
    return value;
  }

  set(key, value) {
    if (this.map.has(key)) this.map.delete(key);
    this.map.set(key, value);
    if (this.map.size > this.limit) {
      const oldest = this.map.keys().next().value; // first key = least recently used
      this.map.delete(oldest);
    }
  }

  keys() {
    return [...this.map.keys()];
  }
}

const cache = new LRUCache(3);
cache.set("a", 1);
cache.set("b", 2);
cache.set("c", 3);
console.log(cache.keys());

cache.get("a"); // "a" is now the most recently used
cache.set("d", 4); // over the limit: "b" (the oldest) is removed
console.log(cache.keys());
console.log(cache.get("b"));
```

Output:

```
[ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]
[ 'c', 'a', 'd' ]
undefined
```

Notes:
- Both `get` and `set` run in constant time, because `Map` lookups, deletes and inserts are constant time.
- Use it to cache API responses, computed thumbnails or database rows when memory is limited.
- The same idea in other languages: Python has `functools.lru_cache`, and Rust's `lru` crate gives the same structure.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
What are memoize and pipe in JavaScript? Show a working implementation of each.
@@@ ASSISTANT
**memoize** remembers the results of a function, so calling it again with the same arguments returns the saved answer instead of recomputing. Use it only for pure functions (same input always gives the same output).

**pipe** connects functions in a row: the output of each becomes the input of the next, which reads left to right like a pipeline.

```js
function memoize(fn) {
  const cache = new Map();
  return (...args) => {
    const key = JSON.stringify(args);
    if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key);
    const result = fn(...args);
    cache.set(key, result);
    return result;
  };
}

let realCalls = 0;
const square = (n) => {
  realCalls++;
  return n * n;
};
const fastSquare = memoize(square);

console.log(fastSquare(9), fastSquare(9), fastSquare(4));
console.log("real calls:", realCalls);

const pipe = (...fns) => (input) => fns.reduce((value, fn) => fn(value), input);

const slugify = pipe(
  (s) => s.trim(),
  (s) => s.toLowerCase(),
  (s) => s.replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-"),
  (s) => s.replace(/^-+|-+$/g, "")
);

console.log(slugify("  Hello, World! Rust & JS  "));
```

Output:

```
81 81 16
real calls: 2
hello-world-rust-js
```

Good to know:
- The cache key here is `JSON.stringify(args)`. That is simple but slow for big arguments, and it cannot handle functions or circular objects.
- A memoized function keeps every result in memory. For long-running programs limit the cache size (see an LRU cache).
- `pipe` makes each step small and testable. Each step is an ordinary function, so you can reuse it elsewhere.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I format numbers, currency, dates and relative times in JavaScript without a library?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Use the built-in `Intl` objects. They know the rules of each language and region, so you do not hand-build formats.

```js
const amount = 1234567.5;

console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(amount));
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }).format(amount));
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("de-DE").format(amount));
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en", { notation: "compact" }).format(1250000));

const date = new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 10, 10, 12, 30));
console.log(new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", { dateStyle: "long", timeZone: "UTC" }).format(date));
console.log(
  new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", {
    hour: "2-digit",
    minute: "2-digit",
    hour12: false,
    timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata",
  }).format(date)
);

const relative = new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat("en", { numeric: "auto" });
console.log(relative.format(-1, "day"));
console.log(relative.format(3, "hour"));

const plural = new Intl.PluralRules("en");
console.log(plural.select(1), plural.select(2));
```

Output:

```
₹12,34,567.50
$1,234,567.50
1.234.567,5
1.3M
10 November 2026
18:00
yesterday
in 3 hours
one other
```

Notes:
- The same number is written differently by region: India groups digits as 12,34,567 and Germany uses a dot for thousands and a comma for decimals.
- Always give a `timeZone` when the exact time matters; otherwise the user's computer time zone is used. `12:30 UTC` is `18:00` in India (UTC+5:30).
- Store money as integers in the smallest unit (paise, cents) in your database, and format only when showing it.
- `Intl.PluralRules` helps with "1 item" vs "2 items" in many languages, not just English.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Show me practical JavaScript regex: find dates, named groups, all matches, replace with a function, and email check.
@@@ ASSISTANT
```js
const text =
  "Order #A-1042 shipped on 2026-11-10 to asha@example.com; order #B-77 on 2026-12-01 to ravi@test.org";

// All dates (the g flag finds every match)
console.log(text.match(/\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/g));

// Named groups: read parts by name
const m = text.match(/(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})-(?<day>\d{2})/);
console.log(m.groups.year, m.groups.month, m.groups.day);

// Every email, using matchAll
console.log([...text.matchAll(/[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+/g)].map((x) => x[0]));

// Capture groups from every match
console.log([...text.matchAll(/#([A-Z])-(\d+)/g)].map(([, letter, num]) => `${letter}${num}`));

// Replace with a function: double every number
console.log("price: 5 and 12".replace(/\d+/g, (n) => String(Number(n) * 2)));

// Simple email check
const isEmail = (s) => /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(s);
console.log(isEmail("a@b.co"), isEmail("a@b"), isEmail("a b@c.com"));
```

Output:

```
[ '2026-11-10', '2026-12-01' ]
2026 11 10
[ 'asha@example.com', 'ravi@test.org' ]
[ 'A1042', 'B77' ]
price: 10 and 24
true false false
```

Cheat sheet:
- `\d` digit, `\w` letter/digit/underscore, `\s` whitespace; `+` one or more, `*` zero or more, `?` optional, `{4}` exactly four.
- `^` start and `$` end of the text; without them, `.test()` is true if the pattern appears anywhere.
- `[^\s@]` means "any character except whitespace and @".
- The email regex only checks the shape. The only real proof that an address works is sending a message to it.
- Never write a regex for a full HTML parser or a very complex format; use a real parser.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I work with JSON in JavaScript: handle parse errors, restore dates, hide fields, and what can't be stringified?
@@@ ASSISTANT
```js
// 1. Parsing invalid JSON throws a SyntaxError. JSON needs double quotes.
try {
  JSON.parse("{'a': 1}");
} catch (error) {
  console.log(error.name);
}

// 2. Dates become strings. Use a "reviver" to turn them back into Date objects.
const raw = '{"name":"Asha","joined":"2026-11-10T00:00:00.000Z","tags":["a","b"]}';
const user = JSON.parse(raw, (key, value) => (key === "joined" ? new Date(value) : value));
console.log(user.joined.getUTCFullYear(), user.joined instanceof Date);

// 3. A "replacer" hides fields; the third argument adds indentation.
const account = { id: 1, name: "Asha", password: "secret" };
console.log(JSON.stringify(account, (key, value) => (key === "password" ? undefined : value), 2));

// 4. Some values are skipped or changed
console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: undefined, c: () => 1, d: new Date(0), e: NaN }));

// 5. Circular references cannot be stringified
const loop = {};
loop.self = loop;
try {
  JSON.stringify(loop);
} catch (error) {
  console.log(error.name);
}
```

Output:

```
SyntaxError
2026 true
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Asha"
}
{"a":1,"d":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","e":null}
TypeError
```

Rules to remember:
- Always wrap `JSON.parse` of outside data (files, network, `localStorage`) in `try/catch`.
- `undefined` and functions are dropped from objects; `NaN` and `Infinity` become `null`; a `Date` becomes an ISO string.
- `Map`, `Set` and `BigInt` are not handled by default: convert them first, for example `[...map]` or `value.toString()`.
- Never put secrets into objects you send to the browser; hiding them in `stringify` is a safety net, not a design.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
What is the difference between debounce and throttle in JavaScript? Give a throttle I can test without waiting.
@@@ ASSISTANT
- **Debounce:** wait until the events stop for N milliseconds, then run once. Good for search boxes and "save after typing".
- **Throttle:** run at most once per N milliseconds while events keep coming. Good for scroll, resize and mouse-move handlers.

This throttle takes the clock as a parameter, so you can test it with a fake clock instead of real waiting:

```js
function throttle(fn, wait, now = Date.now) {
  let last = -Infinity;
  return (...args) => {
    const time = now();
    if (time - last >= wait) {
      last = time;
      return fn(...args);
    }
  };
}

let clock = 0;
const calls = [];
const throttled = throttle((label) => calls.push(label), 100, () => clock);

const events = [[0, "a"], [50, "b"], [99, "c"], [100, "d"], [150, "e"], [210, "f"]];
for (const [time, label] of events) {
  clock = time;
  throttled(label);
}
console.log(calls);
```

Output:

```
[ 'a', 'd', 'f' ]
```

Why: `a` runs at time 0. `b` (50) and `c` (99) come less than 100 ms later, so they are ignored. `d` (100) is exactly 100 ms after `a`, so it runs. `e` (150) is ignored, and `f` (210) runs.

Choosing between them:
- Typing in a search box: debounce (only the final text matters).
- Scrolling, to update a progress bar: throttle (you want regular updates while it happens).
- Passing the clock in as a parameter is a general trick for making time-based code testable.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Why does changing my copied object also change the original in JavaScript? How do I copy objects properly?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Spread (`{ ...obj }`) and `Object.assign` make a **shallow** copy: the top-level properties are copied, but nested objects and arrays are still shared between the copy and the original. Use `structuredClone` for a real deep copy.

```js
const original = {
  name: "Asha",
  address: { city: "Hyderabad" },
  joined: new Date(0),
  tags: ["a"],
};

// Shallow copy: `address` is the very same object in both
const shallow = { ...original };
shallow.address.city = "Pune";
console.log(original.address.city);

// Deep copy: nothing is shared
const deep = structuredClone(original);
deep.address.city = "Delhi";
deep.tags.push("b");
console.log(original.address.city, original.tags);
console.log(deep.joined instanceof Date);

// The JSON trick loses types: a Date becomes a string
const viaJson = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(original));
console.log(typeof viaJson.joined);

// Object.freeze is shallow too
const frozen = Object.freeze({ list: [1] });
frozen.list.push(2); // allowed: only the top level is frozen
frozen.extra = 1; // silently ignored (an error in strict mode)
console.log(frozen);
```

Output:

```
Pune
Pune [ 'a' ]
true
string
{ list: [ 1, 2 ] }
```

Which copy to use:
- Flat object with only numbers, strings and booleans: spread is enough.
- Nested data: `structuredClone(obj)`. It keeps dates, maps and sets, but cannot copy functions.
- In state management (React and similar), do not change nested data in place. Copy each level you change: `{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, city: "Delhi" } }`.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
What are the common date mistakes in JavaScript, and how do I add days or count the days between two dates correctly?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Three traps: months start at 0, a date-only string like `"2026-11-10"` is read as UTC while a string with a time and no zone is read as local time, and invalid dates silently roll over (February 29 in a normal year becomes March 1). Use the UTC methods when you want calendar-day math that does not depend on the computer's time zone.

```js
const d = new Date("2026-11-10"); // date-only string: UTC midnight
console.log(d.toISOString());
console.log(d.getUTCMonth()); // 10: November, because months start at 0
console.log(["Sun", "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat"][d.getUTCDay()]);

function addDays(date, n) {
  const copy = new Date(date); // never change the date you were given
  copy.setUTCDate(copy.getUTCDate() + n);
  return copy;
}
console.log(addDays(d, 30).toISOString().slice(0, 10));

const daysBetween = (a, b) => Math.round((b - a) / 86400000); // 86,400,000 ms in a day
console.log(daysBetween(new Date("2026-11-10"), new Date("2027-01-01")));

// An impossible date rolls over instead of failing
console.log(new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 1, 29)).toISOString().slice(0, 10));
```

Output:

```
2026-11-10T00:00:00.000Z
10
Tue
2026-12-10
52
2026-03-01
```

Tips:
- Subtracting two `Date` objects gives milliseconds. Divide to get days, and use `Math.round` because daylight saving time can make a local day 23 or 25 hours long.
- Store timestamps in UTC (ISO strings or milliseconds) and convert to the user's time zone only for display (`Intl.DateTimeFormat` with `timeZone`).
- For anything complicated (recurring events, time zones, business days), use a library such as `date-fns` or the upcoming `Temporal` API.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I read and write a JSON file in Node.js with async/await, and create the file if it does not exist yet?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Use `fs/promises` and treat "file not found" (`error.code === "ENOENT"`) as an empty result. Re-throw every other error, so real problems are not hidden.

```js
const fs = require("fs/promises");
const os = require("os");
const path = require("path");

async function main() {
  // A temporary folder keeps this demo from touching your real files
  const dir = await fs.mkdtemp(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "demo-"));
  const file = path.join(dir, "notes.json");

  async function readNotes() {
    try {
      return JSON.parse(await fs.readFile(file, "utf8"));
    } catch (error) {
      if (error.code === "ENOENT") return []; // first run: no file yet
      throw error;
    }
  }

  async function addNote(text) {
    const notes = await readNotes();
    notes.push({ id: notes.length + 1, text });
    await fs.writeFile(file, JSON.stringify(notes, null, 2));
    return notes.length;
  }

  console.log(await readNotes());
  await addNote("buy milk");
  await addNote("write data");
  console.log(await readNotes());
  console.log(path.basename(file), path.extname(file));

  await fs.rm(dir, { recursive: true });
}

main();
```

Output:

```
[]
[ { id: 1, text: 'buy milk' }, { id: 2, text: 'write data' } ]
notes.json .json
```

Notes:
- Use `path.join` instead of gluing strings with slashes, so it works on Windows and Linux.
- Pass `"utf8"` to `readFile`, otherwise you get a raw `Buffer` instead of text.
- Two requests writing the same file at the same time can overwrite each other. For a real app use a database such as SQLite, or write to a temporary file and rename it.
- `fs.mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })` creates a folder and any missing parents, and does not fail if it already exists.
@@@ END
